title: JOSEPH COULDN’T CONTROL HIMSELF ANY LONGER—THEN HE SAID FIVE WORDS THAT LEFT HIS BROTHERS TERRIFIED: “I AM JOSEPH.”
paragraphs: JOSEPH COULDN’T CONTROL HIMSELF ANY LONGER—THEN HE SAID FIVE WORDS THAT LEFT HIS BROTHERS TERRIFIED: “I AM JOSEPH.”

They sold him. They lied about him. They buried his name beneath twenty years of silence. Now they stood before the brother they had betrayed—never imagining that the powerful man who held their future in his hands was the very person they had tried to erase. What happened next reveals something breathtaking about the heart of God, the weight of repentance, and the grace that can rewrite even the most shameful chapters of a human life.
“Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me.” — Genesis 45:1 (KJV)
There are some wounds you learn to live with.
Not because they stopped hurting.
Not because you forgot.
But because life kept moving, even when something inside you remained trapped in the moment everything fell apart.
You learned to smile again. You went to work. You paid your bills. You attended church. You answered people when they asked how you were doing.
And somewhere beneath all that normal living was a memory you never quite knew what to do with.
The person who betrayed you.
The family member who abandoned you.
The accusation you never deserved.
The apology that never came.
The years you cannot get back.
Now imagine looking directly into the faces of the people responsible.
Imagine they are standing in front of you, completely unaware of who you are.
Imagine having the power to make them feel every ounce of the pain they once made you feel.
That was Joseph.

And the moment that followed was so overwhelming that the man who had survived slavery, false accusation, imprisonment, and years of separation from his family could no longer contain what was happening inside him.
But before we reach those words—“I am Joseph”—you need to understand why they shook an entire room.
Because this was not merely a family reunion.
This was the collision of guilt and mercy.
Of hidden sin and exposed truth.
Of twenty years of consequences meeting a grace nobody in that room could have earned.
And perhaps, somewhere in Joseph's story, you will recognize your own.
Joseph had once been a seventeen-year-old boy with dreams about the future.
He was loved deeply by his father, Jacob, who gave him a distinctive robe. But within his own household, Joseph was also hated by his brothers.
Genesis 37 does not pretend this family was healthy.
Favoritism had poisoned relationships. Jealousy had become bitterness. Bitterness had hardened into hatred.
When Joseph shared his dreams, his brothers resented him even more.
Then came the day that changed everything.
His father sent him to check on his brothers while they were tending the flocks.
Joseph went looking for family.
Instead, he walked toward betrayal.
His brothers saw him coming from a distance.
Before he reached them, they were already plotting against him.
Think about that.
Joseph was approaching people whose faces he knew, whose voices he recognized, whose blood ran through his own veins.
He had no idea that the people he was walking toward were discussing his destruction.
They stripped him of his robe.
They threw him into a pit.
And while he was helpless, they sat down to eat.
That detail in Genesis 37:25 is almost unbearable.
They were eating while their brother was suffering.
Later, in Genesis 42:21, the brothers themselves remembered something that makes the scene even more heartbreaking.
They recalled seeing the anguish of Joseph's soul when he pleaded with them—and they refused to listen.
He begged.
They heard him.
And they did it anyway.
Eventually, they sold him into slavery for twenty pieces of silver.
Then they deceived their father with Joseph's bloodstained robe, allowing Jacob to believe that his beloved son had been killed by a wild animal.
Joseph was alive.
But to his father, he was dead.
And to his brothers, he was gone.
Maybe you know what it feels like when someone else makes a decision that changes your entire life.
You didn't choose the betrayal.
You didn't choose the abandonment.
You didn't choose the false accusation.
But you were left carrying the consequences.
Joseph was taken to Egypt, far from home, far from his father, far from everything familiar.
Yet Genesis 39:2 tells us something extraordinary.
“And the LORD was with Joseph.”
Not merely when Joseph was comfortable.
Not merely when people treated him fairly.
The Lord was with Joseph in slavery.
And when Joseph faithfully served in Potiphar's household, another injustice came.
Potiphar's wife attempted to seduce him.
Joseph refused.
His reason was not merely fear of consequences. It was reverence for God.
He asked, in Genesis 39:9:
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
Joseph chose faithfulness.
And was falsely accused anyway.
He was thrown into prison.
There is something deeply uncomfortable about this part of Scripture.
Joseph did what was right, yet suffered for it.
We sometimes want the Bible to promise that obedience will immediately make life easier.
But Joseph's story will not allow us to believe that.
Sometimes faithfulness costs you.
Sometimes righteousness is misunderstood.
Sometimes the person who refuses to compromise is the one who ends up behind bars.
And still, Genesis 39:21 says:
“But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy.”
The presence of God did not mean Joseph would never enter a prison.
It meant Joseph had not been abandoned inside it.
Years passed.
Joseph interpreted dreams.
A fellow prisoner who could have remembered him forgot him.
More waiting.
More silence.
More days when the future seemed completely disconnected from the dreams of his youth.
Then, at thirty years old, Joseph stood before Pharaoh.
God enabled him to interpret Pharaoh's dreams, warning of seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine.
Pharaoh placed Joseph over Egypt's administration.
The young man who had been sold as a slave became the ruler entrusted with preserving food for a nation.
But notice something.
Joseph's promotion did not erase his past.
Power does not automatically heal pain.
Success does not guarantee that old wounds disappear.
A person can become respected by strangers while still carrying sorrow connected to family.
Joseph even named his firstborn son Manasseh, saying that God had made him forget his trouble and his father's household (Genesis 41:51).
This did not mean Joseph had lost every memory. His later tears prove otherwise. It expressed the relief God had given him amid years of affliction.
Then famine spread.
And eventually, hunger drove Joseph's brothers to Egypt.
They came searching for food.
They had no idea they were walking into the presence of the brother they had sold.
Genesis 42:6 tells us they bowed before Joseph.
The dreams they once mocked were unfolding before their eyes.
Joseph recognized them.
They did not recognize him.
And here is where the story becomes almost painfully human.
Joseph did not immediately reveal himself.
He spoke harshly to them. He tested their words. He questioned their honesty.
He wanted to know whether they had changed.
Was Benjamin, his younger brother, safe?
Was their father still alive?
Were these still the men who could sacrifice a brother and then return home with a lie?
The narrative does not tell us every thought passing through Joseph's mind. But it shows us that reconciliation did not begin with pretending nothing had happened.
Truth had to come into the light.
The brothers began remembering their guilt.
They spoke of Joseph's anguish.
They acknowledged their wrongdoing.
And Joseph, listening without their knowledge, turned away and wept (Genesis 42:24).
There he was.
The powerful governor of Egypt.
A man who could command servants and soldiers.
A man whose decisions affected the survival of nations.
Turning away to cry.
Because underneath the Egyptian clothing and political authority was still the brother who had begged them to listen.
Please do not miss that.
Sometimes the people who look strongest are carrying stories you know nothing about.
Sometimes the person everyone admires still remembers the day they were rejected.
And sometimes the wounds we think we have buried are waiting for a moment of truth.
Then came the test involving Benjamin.
Joseph arranged circumstances in which Benjamin appeared guilty of stealing his silver cup.
The brothers were brought back.
And Judah—the same Judah who had proposed selling Joseph in Genesis 37:26–27—stepped forward.
He pleaded for Benjamin.
He explained how losing Benjamin would devastate their elderly father.
And then Judah said something remarkable.
“Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren.” — Genesis 44:33 (KJV)
Read that slowly.
Judah offered himself as a slave so that Benjamin could go free.
Years earlier, Judah had helped send one brother into slavery.
Now he was offering to enter slavery in another brother's place.
This did not undo what he had done to Joseph.
But it revealed a profound change in his willingness to protect his brother and spare his father further suffering.
And Joseph heard every word.
He heard Judah speak about their father's grief.
He heard the desperation.
He heard the offer of sacrifice.
And then—
Something broke open.
Genesis 45:1 says:
“Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him.”
The Hebrew expression is powerful.
וְלֹא־יָכֹל יוֹסֵף לְהִתְאַפֵּק
Ve-lo yakhol Yosef lehit'apek.
Literally, the words communicate that Joseph was no longer able to restrain himself.
The verb lehit'apek comes from a Hebrew root associated with restraining or holding oneself back.
This was not a carefully staged political announcement.
Joseph had reached the moment when he could no longer contain his emotions.
He cried out for everyone else to leave.
The Egyptian attendants withdrew.
The room was emptied of outsiders.
Only Joseph and his brothers remained.
Then Genesis 45:2 tells us:
“And he wept aloud: and the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard.”
He did not merely shed a quiet tear.
He wept so loudly that people outside the room heard him.
The man who had learned to survive betrayal was crying in front of the very people who betrayed him.
And then came the words.
The words his brothers never expected to hear.
The words that would pull the past into the present.
אֲנִי יוֹסֵף
Ani Yosef.
“I am Joseph.”
Genesis 45:3.
Only two words in Hebrew.
But what those two words carried was almost beyond comprehension.
I am the brother you hated.
I am the boy you stripped.
I am the one you threw into the pit.
I am the one whose cries you ignored.
I am the one you sold.
I am the son whose supposed death broke our father's heart.
I am Joseph.
Alive.
Standing before you.
And suddenly, every lie they had lived with came face-to-face with the truth.
Joseph continued:
“Doth my father yet live?”
And the Bible says:
“And his brethren could not answer him; for they were troubled at his presence.” — Genesis 45:3 (KJV)
The Hebrew word used to describe their reaction comes from בָּהַל (bahal), a verb expressing alarm, dismay, or being overwhelmed.
They were not simply surprised.
They were deeply shaken.
Imagine their minds racing.
Joseph?
Alive?
Here?
The man who controls the food?
The man who holds our future?
The brother we sold?
How do you explain twenty years of silence in a single moment?
How do you defend what you did when the person you wounded is standing directly in front of you?
And how do you ask for mercy when you know you have no right to demand it?
This is where Joseph's story begins to expose something about every human heart.
Because the brothers were not the only people who had a past they could not undo.
We all have things we wish we could take back.
Words spoken in anger.
Trust broken through selfishness.
Moments when jealousy controlled us.
Decisions made in secret.
People we hurt while justifying ourselves.
Maybe your story is not as dramatic as Joseph's brothers.
But if we are truthful before God, none of us can claim to have lived without sin.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That includes the respectable.
The religious.
The successful.
The people who know the right Bible verses.
The people who have learned how to look spiritually healthy while hiding what is happening inside.
And this is why the next sentence from Joseph is so extraordinary.
He did not begin with a threat.
He did not demand that they fall to their knees.
He did not use his authority to humiliate them.
Genesis 45:4 says:
“And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you.”
Come near.
Can you imagine how difficult those steps must have felt?
They knew what they had done.
They knew he remembered.
They knew they could not undo it.
And yet the brother they had pushed away was calling them closer.
Then Joseph said:
“I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.”
He did not erase the truth.
He named it.
Whom ye sold.
There was no pretending the betrayal never happened.
No rewriting history to make the guilty comfortable.
No declaration that their cruelty had somehow become good.
Joseph's mercy did not require calling evil righteous.
And that matters.
Because biblical forgiveness is not the same as denying harm.
It does not require victims to pretend that abuse, betrayal, or injustice was harmless.
It does not mean trust must be restored instantly or that every broken relationship must return to its former condition.
Joseph had already observed his brothers over time, and the narrative had shown significant evidence of changed behavior.
Grace and truth were standing together.
And then Joseph revealed how he understood God's work through the suffering.
Genesis 45:5:
“Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.”
Those words are astonishing.
But they must be understood carefully.
Joseph was not saying that selling a brother into slavery was acceptable.
He was not saying that God approved of their jealousy or cruelty.
He was recognizing that God's sovereign purposes had prevailed even through human evil.
Later, Joseph would explain this even more clearly in Genesis 50:20:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”
The Hebrew makes the contrast especially striking.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה
Attem chashavtem alai ra'ah.
“You intended evil against me.”
אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Elohim chashavah letovah.
“God intended it for good.”
The same Hebrew root, chashav, appears in both statements, emphasizing the contrast between human intention and divine purpose.
The brothers intended harm.
God intended good.
The evil remained evil.
But it did not have the final word.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
What happened to you may have been genuinely wrong.
The betrayal may have been real.
The damage may still affect your life.
You may still need boundaries, wise counsel, accountability, or time to heal.
But the people who wounded you do not possess ultimate authority over what God can do with your future.
Their sin is not stronger than His sovereignty.
Their cruelty is not greater than His wisdom.
Their rejection cannot cancel His faithfulness.
Joseph's life was not proof that every painful story ends with wealth, influence, or a public apology.
Scripture makes no such promise.
It was proof that God was faithfully working through circumstances Joseph himself could not control.
And now look again at that room.
Joseph could have taken revenge.
Instead, he offered reassurance and provision.
He told his brothers to bring their father and households to Egypt, where they could survive the remaining years of famine.
He wept upon Benjamin's neck.
He kissed all his brothers and wept over them.
And afterward, his brothers talked with him.
The silence had finally been broken.
The family that had been torn apart by jealousy was being drawn into a future none of them could have imagined.
But there is an even greater story unfolding through Joseph's life.
One that leads us beyond Egypt.
Beyond the pit.
Beyond the palace.
All the way to Jesus Christ.
Joseph is not Jesus, and we must never pretend that every detail of Joseph's life is a direct prophecy about Christ.
Yet Scripture allows us to recognize meaningful patterns in God's redemptive work.
Joseph was rejected by his brothers, suffered unjustly, and later became an instrument through whom God preserved lives.
Jesus Christ came to His own and was rejected (John 1:11).
He was innocent, yet condemned.
He was betrayed, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
But unlike Joseph, Jesus was not merely a righteous sufferer whom God later elevated.
He is the eternal Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Joseph helped preserve people from physical starvation.
Jesus came to rescue sinners from sin and death and to give eternal life.
Joseph's suffering became part of God's plan to preserve a family.
Christ's death and resurrection accomplished the redemption that no human being could ever achieve.
And when Jesus hung upon the cross, He prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34 (KJV)
Those words do not mean that everyone was automatically forgiven apart from repentance and faith.
They reveal the extraordinary mercy of the Savior who interceded even for those participating in His crucifixion.
At the cross, the depth of human sin met the immeasurable love of God.
Acts 2:23 teaches that Jesus was delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, yet was crucified through the actions of lawless men.
Human evil was real.
Human responsibility was real.
And God's saving purpose was not defeated.
Do you see the connection?
What Joseph's brothers meant for evil, God worked through for the preservation of life.
What sinful humanity did to Jesus was evil beyond measure.
Yet through His willing sacrifice and victorious resurrection, God accomplished salvation for all who believe.
The cross was not evil becoming good.
It was God accomplishing the greatest good through the very evil human beings committed against His Son.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your past was harmless.
Not that your sins were small.
Not that forgiveness is cheap.
But that Jesus Christ bore the penalty of sin, rose from the dead, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Some of you are reading this as Joseph.
You were wounded.
You were betrayed.
You have carried pain that people around you never fully understood.
You have wondered whether God saw what happened.
You have struggled to reconcile His goodness with your suffering.
And perhaps you have mistaken the length of your waiting for evidence of His absence.
But Joseph's story reminds you that God's presence is not measured by how quickly circumstances improve.
The Lord was with Joseph in the house of Potiphar.
The Lord was with Joseph in prison.
The Lord was with Joseph when he stood before Pharaoh.
And the Lord was still working when Joseph's brothers returned.
If you belong to Christ, you are not forgotten simply because your circumstances are difficult.
God has not promised you Joseph's earthly position.
He has promised something greater: that nothing can separate His people from His love in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38–39).
And some of you are reading this as Joseph's brothers.
You are carrying guilt.
There is something you did.
Something you said.
Someone you hurt.
Something you have hidden so carefully that even people close to you do not know the truth.
Maybe you have spent years hoping the past would stay buried.
Maybe you attend church and sing about grace while secretly wondering whether God could forgive someone who knows better and still sinned.
Maybe you have confused hiding your sin with escaping its consequences.
But listen.
The answer is not to become better at pretending.
The answer is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is grounded in Jesus Christ and His atoning work.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what you did.
It involves turning from sin toward God.
Where possible and appropriate, it includes making things right with those you have harmed.
And it means trusting the mercy of Christ rather than trying to earn forgiveness through endless self-punishment.
The brothers could not undo the sale of Joseph.
But they could acknowledge their wrongdoing and begin living differently.
You cannot rewrite yesterday by your own power.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to be the master of tomorrow.
And perhaps the most dangerous place to be is neither Joseph's pain nor his brothers' guilt.
Perhaps it is standing outside the whole story, convinced you do not need grace.
Because you have never sold a brother.
You have never committed a scandal that became public.
You have never done anything you consider unforgivable.
But the Gospel does not divide humanity into people who need a Savior and people who do not.
It declares that every one of us needs Jesus.
The person whose sin is publicly exposed.
And the person whose pride is privately concealed.
The one who has been running from God for twenty years.
And the one who has been sitting in church for twenty years without truly surrendering.
We all come to the same cross.
Empty-handed.
Unable to save ourselves.
Dependent on grace.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
No donation that can earn salvation.
No religious activity that can replace repentance and faith.
No amount of good deeds that can erase the need for the blood of Jesus.
Salvation is God's gift.
And that is precisely why the Gospel is so beautiful.
You do not have to pretend you were never guilty.
You do not have to claim your wounds never hurt.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect life before coming to Christ.
You come honestly.
You repent.
You believe.
You entrust yourself to the Savior who died and rose again.
And He begins transforming you from the inside out.
Maybe today, your prayer is not eloquent.
Maybe all you can say is:
“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding.”
Or:
“Jesus, I am still angry.”
Or:
“Lord, I do not know how to forgive.”
Or:
“Father, I have sinned, and I need Your mercy.”
You do not need impressive words.
You need a sincere heart turned toward Christ.
If this story has uncovered something you have been carrying, do not rush past that conviction.
Sit with Scripture.
Bring it before God.
And if you need to speak with a trustworthy pastor, mature Christian, or qualified counselor about deep wounds, please do so. Seeking wise help does not diminish your faith.
Perhaps there is someone you need to forgive, while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Perhaps there is someone you need to ask for forgiveness.
Perhaps there is a hidden sin you need to confess.
Perhaps you have been trying to heal without allowing the truth into the room.
Remember what Joseph did.
He did not erase the past.
He brought it into the light.
And grace met the truth there.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is so close to our hearts:
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because every relationship can be restored.
Not because every consequence is removed.
But because through Jesus Christ, sin and shame need not have the final word over a repentant sinner's life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
What a promise.
Not that you become someone who never had a past.
But that in Christ, you become someone whose deepest identity is no longer defined by that past.
Joseph's brothers entered that room fearing the man they had betrayed.
They left having encountered a brother who extended mercy.
And every time I return to this passage, one thought stays with me.
Joseph's brothers had spent years believing they had permanently removed him from their lives.
But God was working through Joseph to preserve the very family that had rejected him.
They had no idea how much their future would depend on the brother they once despised.
And how much more do we need Jesus—the Savior humanity rejected, yet whom God raised from the dead?
There is no greater mercy than the mercy offered through Christ.
There is no deeper cleansing than the forgiveness purchased by His blood.
There is no more lasting hope than His resurrection.
And there is no better day than today to stop hiding from the One who already knows the truth about you.
If you have been far from God, turn to Jesus.
If you have been living with unconfessed sin, repent.
If you are exhausted from pretending, bring your real condition before Him.
If you are a wounded believer, ask Him for the strength to keep walking in truth, wisdom, and grace.
And if you are growing in Christ, remember that discipleship does not end with one emotional moment.
We need Scripture tomorrow.
We need prayer tomorrow.
We need fellowship, correction, encouragement, and spiritual nourishment long after the tears have dried.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish another emotional article that people forget after scrolling.
But to continually point people toward Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, genuine repentance, biblical understanding, and a life of faithful discipleship.
You never know who might be reading quietly.
Someone who has not opened a Bible in years.
Someone struggling with guilt.
Someone grieving a family betrayal.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to church.
Someone who desperately needs to know that forgiveness through Jesus Christ is still possible.
A simple share can place the truth of Scripture before someone who might never have searched for it themselves.
And if one particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with care—or sending this privately if their situation is sensitive.
Not to expose their pain.
Not to embarrass them.
But to remind them that they have not been forgotten.
Not because every word here is easy to hear, but because there may come a day when you need to revisit Genesis 45 and remember that God can work through circumstances you never would have chosen.
And please, do not leave without joining the conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details.
A few honest words can be the beginning of meaningful prayer and encouragement among believers.
Your experience may encourage someone who is struggling to believe that change is possible.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully, sin is not excused, grace is not cheapened, and people are encouraged to grow beyond emotional inspiration into genuine obedience to God.
And for those who feel called to help sustain and expand this mission, I want to speak plainly and gratefully.
Producing biblical content, maintaining resources, reaching more people, and continually developing discipleship materials requires ongoing support.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, love, service, generosity, and a life surrendered to His will.
It can help us continue preparing Scripture-centered messages, sharing Christian resources, and reaching readers who may be struggling spiritually or encountering the Gospel for the first time.
Our desire is that nobody would mistake financial ability for spiritual worth.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The Word of God is not reserved for paying supporters.
And the mercy of Jesus Christ is freely offered to all who repent and believe.
Pray for this work.
Encourage people to open their Bibles.
Most importantly, live out the truth you are reading.
Because the goal is not merely a larger audience.
The goal is people being directed to Jesus Christ.
People learning to repent.
People growing in grace.
People understanding Scripture.
People discovering that a life surrendered to Christ can truly be transformed.
Joseph is standing before his brothers.
They are terrified.
The truth is out.
The past cannot be changed.
And the future is entirely uncertain.
Then he speaks.
Ani Yosef.
I am Joseph.
The brother they thought they had erased is alive.
The man they wronged is extending mercy.
The family they shattered is being given an opportunity for reconciliation.
And beyond that room, a greater story is still unfolding.
Through the family of Jacob, God would continue His covenant promises.
Through the tribe of Judah, the promised Messiah would eventually come.
And through Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, salvation would be proclaimed to the nations.
What an astonishing testimony to the faithfulness of God.
Human beings sinned.
Families fractured.
Years were lost.
Tears were shed.
But the Lord remained faithful to His purposes.
So whatever side of Joseph's story you recognize yourself in today, remember this:
You may be the wounded one who needs God's strength to heal.
You may be the guilty one who needs to repent.
You may be the weary one who has almost stopped hoping.
But Jesus Christ is sufficient for the sinner who comes to Him in faith, and faithful to sustain those who belong to Him.
Do not let the shame of yesterday keep you from turning to the Savior today.
Do not let bitterness convince you that revenge is the only way forward.
Do not let suffering persuade you that God has ceased to be good.
And do not confuse the end of a painful chapter with the end of God's ability to work in your life.
Because the most unforgettable part of Joseph's story is not that he became powerful enough to punish his brothers.
It is that, when the truth finally came into the light, mercy was possible.
And the greatest hope of our own story is not that we can somehow become powerful enough to repair everything we have broken.
It is that Jesus Christ has accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
The hands that once held Joseph's fate were the hands of sinful men—but the hands that hold your eternal hope are the nail-scarred hands of the risen Christ.
